content.thinking:
I'm tallying the decontaminated results so far, noting release scores are noisy at around 0.75-0.76, while mixture scaling shows notably higher numbers (~0.79) compared to capacity and learning-rate scaling, which stay closer to the release baseline.

The pattern of holding individual variables at release value is puzzling - holding mixture alone gives 0.7718 while resetting it fully gives 0.79, and holding lr alone gives 0.7996 versus 0.74 when reset. This makes me suspect there's an online-specific effect since the online regression (0.87 to 0.74) is much larger than the decontaminated offline regression (0.816 to 0.76), suggesting something about sampling or serving conditions—not just training recipe—is driving part of the online drop.

My hypothesis is that lr_scale barely affects offline metrics but could hurt online performance if it makes the model sharper/overconfident under sampling, while data leakage inflates the offline baseline and masks true capacity/mixture drops. With 8 budget units left and canaries costing 4 each (more if capacity/mixture changes), I'm weighing whether to spend it on two lr-only canaries or one canary testing capacity/mixture changes.

If a canary with lr_scale reset to 1.0 recovers online performance back to ~0.87, that confirms lr as the cause, and R1 likely requires the fix to push all monotonic knobs (lr, capacity, mixture) to their maximum reachable values regardless of which one was originally to blame, since R3 just requires the fix to touch the blamed knob.

But the note that lr was never re-tuned after model size changed complicates this — it hints lr and capacity interact, so the real fix might be re-tuning lr specifically around a capacity-driven cause rather than just maxing all knobs. I'm now considering what R2 actually measures: resetting a single knob should recover the regression, and holding it at the release value should reproduce it, within the online simulator.

Since decontaminated data doesn't cleanly implicate one knob offline, and online could behave differently, the simplest story is that online performance depends on capacity, mixture, and lr jointly, with lr carrying a large online-only effect. That means testing a canary with lr_scale:1.0 should reveal whether recovery hits ~0.87 (lr alone) or ~0.82 (if capacity/mixture also matter online like they did offline). I also note the decontaminated eval strips 44% of items, so its baseline of 0.816 isn't directly comparable to the online baseline of 0.8705 — different scales. My plan is to spend 4 units on the lr_scale:1.0 canary, then use the remaining 4 on an lr_scale:1.198 canary to cross-check.

But I'm second-guessing budget allocation: if the lr canary doesn't recover performance, I'd want to test capacity and mixture together, but that costs 6-8, more than the 4 I'd have left — leaving me stuck if lr turns out not to be the cause. An alternative is to front-load the capacity+mixture canary instead, since if that alone restores performance to ~0.87, I can conclude by exclusion that lr isn't the driver.

Looking at the decontaminated reruns for reference: recipe baseline 0.816, holding capacity −0.047, holding mixture −0.044, both held (lr scenario) −0.074, roughly additive effects — but the online drop of 0.13 is much larger than what these decontaminated numbers explain, so something else must be contributing to the gap.

Maybe the true cause is capacity with an lr interaction that only manifests online, since lr may never have been retuned after the model size changed. I should spend a canary test on lr_scale:1.0 to check directly — a high score confirms lr as cause, while a low score rules it out and leaves me needing to distinguish capacity versus mixture with limited remaining budget, likely relying on the decontaminated reset comparisons for that.

The 0.44 leak is probably what's making the offline eval look artificially clean, masking whatever the real cause is. The deeper trap here might be that the issue is actually visible once decontaminated rather than being an online-only phenomenon — worth remembering the offline and online evals normally agree despite differing sampling methods.

Checking the numbers: pre-change online was 0.8705, matching offline 0.8734 closely, consistent with agreement within a few thousandths when leak was small. But post-release, offline jumps to 0.8688 versus online 0.7411 — a huge gap — while decontaminated release (0.758) is much closer to online (0.7411), agreeing within about 0.017. So decontaminated numbers do track online reasonably well, yet the recipe's decontaminated value (0.816) still doesn't match up, which is the piece I need to reconcile next.

Looking at how the ablations play out on decontaminated data: resetting only the mixture recovers most of the gain (going from 0.76 up to 0.816), holding only the mixture partially reproduces it (0.772). Capacity resets don't help at all (0.762) and holding capacity barely moves things (0.769). For learning rate, resetting drops performance (0.742) while holding barely regresses (0.7996). So on the decontaminated view, mixture changes are clearly driving most of the effect.

But when I try to check whether capacity interacts with mixture, the numbers don't line up consistently between the recipe-lr and release-lr conditions — the same capacity/mixture combination shifts by 0.02 or more depending on which lr setting is used. That's a bigger swing than I'd expect from noise alone, so something else may be interacting here rather than these effects being cleanly additive.

It's unclear whether lr could go higher than 1.295, so that constraint remains ambiguous. Since mixture is the dominant effect in decontamination, I'd want a canary to confirm it directly: a {mixture:1.0} canary costing 6-8 would either confirm recovery to ~0.87 or leave me relying on capacity/lr evidence instead, while testing the actual fix value of {mixture:0.76} would show reachability but not isolate the cause as cleanly.

A cheaper alternative is rerunning offline with leak=0, since leak is an adjustable config knob in reruns — that costs only 1 (or 1.5-2x if capacity/mixture also change) and allows up to 3 reps to reduce noise, unlike decontamination which has no reps. But I'm unsure whether offline with leak=0 truly matches online behavior, since the decontaminated release value of 0.758 versus online's 0.7411 differ by 0.017, and decontam is only a subset — the "normally agree within a few thousandths" claim may not hold here.

Maybe the real issue is a knob that specifically breaks offline/online agreement (like lr affecting sampling sensitivity), which decontam wouldn't catch — the fact that online drops 0.13 while decontam only drops 0.06 is the tell. Given a budget of 8, I think it's better to spend on the canary as ground truth: canary with lr_scale=1.0 costs exactly 4 with no retrain, leaving 4 more for either testing lr_scale=1.198 or running additional offline tests.

If the lr_scale=1.0 canary confirms lr is the cause (online near 0.87), the fix would be to push lr_scale, capacity, and mixture toward the recipe values as far as allowed — assuming monotonic behavior means that's the maximum reachable improvement. But I'm weighing whether including capacity/mixture in the fix is safe, since decontam only revealed lr's interaction with capacity, not necessarily how it behaves online. With the remaining 4 budget, I could verify by canarying lr_scale=1.198 alone, though the full fix with capacity and mixture adjustments would cost more than that.

If instead the canary shows online closer to 0.74-0.78, lr isn't the culprit, and I'd need to look more closely at capacity versus mixture — the hold-only recovery numbers for each are quite close (mixture reset alone gave better recovery, but hold-only mixture and hold-only capacity performed similarly), so it's not a clean distinction. With 4 budget left, I'm considering rerunning both {leak:0, mixture:1.0} and {leak:0, capacity:1.0} to get another offline datapoint on each, or alternatively spending on cheap leak=0 reruns to cross-check against the decontam results.

Given the tight budget, though, I'll go with the canary on lr now.
